title: If thou wilt (Mark 1:40–45)
hookLine: a leper kneels, and Jesus, moved with compassion, touches him

cards: Leviticus spells out the rule. A person with leprosy goes with clothes loose and head bare, covers the mouth, and cries out unclean, so others keep their distance. That person lives alone, outside the camp.
No hand on the shoulder. No embrace at the door. In today's story, a man living under that rule walks straight up to Jesus, kneels, and says a sentence that begins with three small words.

teach.b: First, the man. Under the law of Moses he's meant to keep his distance, calling out his warning. So he shouldn't be anywhere near Jesus.
He comes anyway. In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." He doesn't doubt Jesus can.
He isn't sure Jesus wants to. Second, the touch. "And Jesus having compassion on him, stretched forth his hand; and touching him, saith to him: I will. Be thou made clean."
He touches him before he heals him. He didn't need to; elsewhere Jesus heals with a word. And under the law, touching a leper made you unclean too.
Jesus reaches out anyway. For a man who lived outside the camp, the touch may have been the first healing. Third, the word compassion.
Mark's Greek is splanchnistheis, from the word for the inward parts: moved in the gut, a feeling from deep inside.
Before he says a word, Jesus is moved. Fourth, the swap. Jesus tells the man to show himself to the priest, as Moses commanded, and to tell no one.

teach.h: I WILL. BE THOU MADE CLEAN.
teach.b: The man tells everyone. Now Jesus can't openly enter a town, and stays out in deserted places. The man is back inside; Jesus is outside.
Centuries later, Saint Francis of Assisi wrote that the Lord led him among lepers, and that what had seemed bitter was turned to sweetness; early stories say he kissed one.
This week began with the psalm about being known, and ends with a hand reaching out to touch.

how: Catholics hear the healing of the leper at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and the Church honors saints who served people with leprosy, such as Francis of Assisi and Damien of Molokai.

o: afraid of catching the man's illness
moved with compassion, from the gut

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the leper doubted Jesus could heal him
he said thou canst. what he wasn't sure of was whether Jesus wanted to.
Jesus told the healed man to show himself to the priest
as Moses commanded, and to tell no one.
the man kept quiet as Jesus asked
he told everyone, and Jesus had to stay out in deserted places.

games.q: a man with leprosy kneels in front of you and says: if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean. the law says touching him makes you unclean. what does Jesus do?
o: heal him with a word from a safe distance.
reach out and touch him, and say I will.
send him to the priest first.
games.why: "stretched forth his hand; and touching him, saith to him: I will. Be thou made clean." the touch comes before the healing.

practice: Think of someone who doesn't get touched much, an older neighbor who lives alone, a grandparent in a care home, someone sick or grieving, a kid who's been left out, and see their face.
If you pray, hold them before God and say the leper's words for them: if thou wilt. If you don't, decide how you might reach them: a hand on the arm, a hug, or a visit.

wordCard.voice: Splanchnistheis. Mark's Greek word for moved with compassion, from the gut, what Jesus felt before he touched the leper who said, if thou wilt. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: moved with compassion, from splanchna, the inward parts, the gut.

carryVoice: Your line: he touched him. The week ran from thou hast searched me and Alleluia into Mark: the gospel, the desert, the nets, Capernaum, and now a touch. Day one hundred ninety-six, done.
